articles.headline: U.S. Designates Eight Individuals and 22 Entities in Iran's Shadow Banking Network
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has imposed sanctions on eight individuals and 22 entities across Iran, the UAE, Hong Kong, and Türkiye. These designations are part of 'Operation Economic Outcast' and target a vast shadow banking network accused of facilitating Iranian trade payments and sanctions evasion.

The sanctioned network includes currency exchange firms, bank-affiliated 'rahbar' companies, and overseas front companies. These entities are believed to move billions of dollars through the international financial system, supporting Iran's remaining foreign trade and circumventing U.S. restrictions.

The action aims to disrupt the financial infrastructure underpinning Iran's illicit financial activities, which a recent Treasury Department study estimated to have facilitated approximately $14.7 billion in transactions between January 2025 and August 2026.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran Designations and Clarifies Cuba Sanctions FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations related to Iran, alongside the issuance of updated Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) concerning Cuba sanctions. The Iran designations are part of ongoing efforts to counter illicit financial activities supporting the Iranian regime.

The Cuba FAQs, specifically FAQs 1277 and 1278, clarify that OFAC's sanctions authority covering Cuba's manufacturing, technology, electronics, and marine sectors does not automatically sanction all persons operating in those sectors.
The guidance further confirms that authorized activities involving Cuba's marine sector, including payments to Cuban ports for authorized trade and certain humanitarian transactions, may continue.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Cyber-related Designations, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related illicit activities. These actions aim to disrupt global criminal networks and protect the U.S. financial system from abuse.
In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License, providing authorizations for certain transactions related to illicit drug trade sanctions.

Additionally, OFAC issued an amended Russia-related General License (General License 131L) and updated Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs 1224 and 1225), specifically authorizing certain transactions related to negotiating and entering into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH, along with related maintenance activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals for Counter Terrorism Activities
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations under its counter terrorism authorities. These actions target individuals and entities found to be supporting terrorist organizations and their activities globally.

Among the designations, OFAC targeted the Lebanon-based Wa Ta'awanu Association and its founder, Afif Abdel Rida Chouman, for allegedly supporting Hizballah under the guise of humanitarian assistance.

The action also included members of a Lebanon- and Türkiye-based gold and cash smuggling network, which OFAC identified as being tied to Hizballah and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Qods Force (IRGC-Qods Force).

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Joint Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a round of designations targeting individuals and entities involved in both counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. This action underscores the interconnectedness of various illicit networks and the U.S. government's commitment to disrupting them.
These designations aim to sever financial and material support to organizations and individuals that pose threats to international security through drug trafficking and terrorist acts.
The specific individuals and entities targeted were not immediately detailed in the initial announcement but fall under OFAC's broader mandates to combat these illicit activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designation List
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an update to its Iran designation list. This action is part of the ongoing 'Operation Economic Outcast,' which aims to sever Iran's remaining financial lifelines.

The update includes modifications to existing listings or additions of new individuals and entities involved in activities that support the Iranian regime, particularly those related to its petroleum, petrochemical, and aviation sectors.
These continuous updates reflect the U.S. government's commitment to maintaining pressure on Iran's financial networks and preventing the financing of terrorism and nuclear proliferation.

articles.headline: U.S. Imposes New Iran-Related Sanctions Targeting Financial Services Companies
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a new round of Iran-related sanctions, specifically targeting eight Canada-based financial services companies.
These designations are part of a broader effort to disrupt financial networks that support the Iranian regime and its illicit activities.

The action follows previous sanctions aimed at Iran's shadow banking networks and oil trustees, indicating a continued focus on limiting Tehran's access to foreign currency and international financial systems.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Issues Cuba-related Determination
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting cyber-related actors and transnational criminal organizations. These actions aim to combat malicious cyber activities and disrupt global criminal enterprises.

In addition to these designations, OFAC also issued new Cuba designations and published a Cuba-related determination. This determination likely clarifies or expands upon existing sanctions against Cuba.

The specific details of the Cuba designations and determination were not immediately available but are expected to further restrict certain transactions or entities associated with the Cuban government.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations, Amends Venezuela General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations and updates to certain Iran-related listings. These actions are part of the ongoing U.S. strategy to exert economic pressure on the Iranian regime.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC published an Iran-related OFAC Alert, likely providing guidance or warnings regarding potential sanctions evasion tactics or high-risk activities involving Iran.
Furthermore, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question, indicating adjustments to existing sanctions policies concerning Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Iran-related General License. This amendment likely modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.
General Licenses typically permit activities that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs, and amendments can either expand or narrow the scope of such authorized transactions.
The specific details of this amended General License were not immediately available but are expected to be published on the OFAC website.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $1,529,685 for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based networking solutions provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations (URSR).

The violations stemmed from the company's Russian subsidiary processing and fulfilling purchase orders for networking equipment and services to a blocked Russian defense manufacturer, MMZA, between March 2018 and March 2022.

OFAC determined that the violations were egregious but voluntarily self-disclosed, and the settlement amount reflects the company's substantial remedial measures and cooperation. The Department of Justice also announced a parallel non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Pays $11,662,930 to OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to settle its potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of multiple OFAC sanctions programs. These programs include those targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The apparent violations occurred when Bank of America processed payments involving blocked banks, failed to appropriately prioritize alerts for customers matching blocked persons, did not promptly update watchlists, and mishandled business accounts associated with blocked persons due to human error.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were non-egregious but largely not voluntarily self-disclosed. This settlement is part of a larger coordinated enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury Department, which also included significant penalties from FinCEN and the OCC.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015 for Narcotics Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based logistics company and freight forwarder, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC counter narcotics sanctions and reporting obligations.

The violations occurred when Pegasus arranged for the shipment of a customized sugar packet-filling machine from a designated Chinese supplier, Youli Technology Development Co., Ltd., without adequately identifying the supplier as sanctioned. Pegasus had only screened the supplier's new name, missing other identifiers.

Additionally, Pegasus initially failed to respond fully to an OFAC administrative subpoena. OFAC determined the violations were non-egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, but credited Pegasus for extensive remedial measures.

articles.headline: Individual Pays $1,427,230 to OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has agreed to pay $1,427,230 to settle potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations. The specific details of the violations and the sanctions program involved were not immediately disclosed in the summary.
This enforcement action highlights OFAC's continued focus on holding individuals accountable for sanctions breaches, alongside corporate entities.
The settlement amount reflects OFAC's assessment of the severity of the violations and any mitigating or aggravating factors present in the case.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Settles for $60,764 Over Iran Sanctions Violations
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc., a Wisconsin-based manufacturer of weighing equipment, has agreed to pay $60,764 to settle its and its Italian subsidiary's potential civil liability for eight apparent violations of OFAC sanctions on Iran.

The violations occurred between July 2019 and November 2021 when the Italian subsidiary, Dini Argeo S.r.l., exported weighing equipment to a distributor in the UAE, knowing the goods were ultimately destined for an end-user in Iran.

Despite Rice Lake having instructed its subsidiary to cease sales to Iran after the revocation of General License H in 2018, Dini continued indirect sales through a middleman. OFAC held Rice Lake responsible for its subsidiary's actions.

articles.headline: FTI Consulting, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $1,050,000
body: FTI Consulting, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,050,000 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations. The specific details of the violations were not immediately available in the summary.
This settlement underscores OFAC's enforcement efforts across various industries and its expectation for robust compliance programs.
The resolution reflects the company's cooperation and any remedial measures undertaken to address the underlying issues that led to the apparent violations.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Pays $275,000,000 for Iran Sanctions Violations
body: Adani Enterprises Limited (AEL), an India-based multinational company, has agreed to pay $275,000,000 to settle its potential civil liability for 32 apparent violations of OFAC's Iran sanctions regulations.

Between November 2023 and June 2025, AEL purchased shipments of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) from a Dubai-based trader that purported to supply Omani and Iraqi gas. However, red flags indicated the LPG actually originated from Iran.

AEL caused U.S. financial institutions to process 32 U.S. dollar-denominated payments totaling approximately $192,104,044 for these shipments. OFAC determined the violations were egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, but credited AEL for substantial cooperation and remedial measures.

articles.headline: TradeStation Securities, Inc. Settles for $1,110,661 Over Multiple Sanctions Violations
body: TradeStation Securities, Inc., a Florida-headquartered brokerage firm, has agreed to pay $1,110,661 to settle its potential civil liability for 481 apparent violations of multiple OFAC sanctions programs.

For nearly a year, from June 21, 2021, to June 15, 2022, TradeStation provided investment services to customers located in Iran, Syria, and the Crimea region of Ukraine, enabling them to execute securities-related transactions.

The violations were attributed to compliance control failures, including issues with geo-blocking controls and a lack of oversight from sanctions compliance personnel. OFAC determined the violations were non-egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed, and the settlement reflects the significant remedial measures implemented by TradeStation.

articles.headline: Individual Settles with OFAC for $3,777,000 for Syria Sanctions Violations
body: A U.S. citizen residing abroad has agreed to pay $3,777,000 to settle potential civil liability for 20 apparent violations of the Syrian Sanctions Regulations.
The violations occurred between 2018 and 2021, though specific details of the individual's activities were not immediately provided.
This enforcement action highlights OFAC's reach to U.S. persons globally and its commitment to enforcing sanctions against the Syrian regime.

articles.headline: IMG Academy, LLC Pays $1,720,000 for Counternarcotics Sanctions Violations
body: IMG Academy, LLC, a Florida-based school and athletic training facility, has agreed to pay $1,720,000 to settle its potential civil liability for 89 apparent violations of OFAC counternarcotics sanctions.

Over a five-year period, IMG Academy entered into tuition enrollment agreements and processed payments with two individuals designated under the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Designation Act due to their ties to a sanctioned Mexican drug cartel.

OFAC found that IMG Academy recklessly disregarded U.S. sanctions requirements by failing to conduct basic sanctions screening, allowing designated individuals to access U.S. academic and athletic training services and the U.S. financial system. The violations were deemed non-egregious, and the settlement reflects the academy's substantial cooperation and remedial measures.

articles.headline: Iranian Rial Plunges to Record Low Following New U.S. Sanctions
body: The Iranian rial has fallen to a record low against the U.S. dollar on the black market, a day after Washington announced fresh sanctions targeting Iran's financial networks. The dollar reached 2.856 million rials, or 285,600 tomans, on Tehran's open market.

The U.S. Treasury Department's latest measures, announced on Monday, targeted more than two dozen Iranian currency exchange businesses, companies, and individuals believed to be part of the country's 'shadow banking' network.

Iranian Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati dismissed the sanctions, stating that the targeted Iran Currency and Gold Exchange Center is merely a platform for registering transactions. The rial's depreciation comes amid persistently high inflation, with consumer prices rising 88.7% year-on-year in October.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
